sections.text: Sometimes the same logic works for many types. Swapping two values does not care whether they are numbers or words. Writing one copy of the function for every type would be a lot of repeated code. A generic function is written once and works for many types.

You make a function generic by adding a type parameter in angle brackets after its name. By convention it is called T, short for "type". T is a placeholder: each time you call the function, Rust fills it in with a real type.

<T> after the name declares the placeholder. After that, T can be used like any type in the parameters and the return type. (T, T) is a tuple holding two values of the same type, and pair.0 and pair.1 pick its parts. In the first call T becomes i32, in the second &str, in the third String. You never write the real type: Rust works it out from the arguments. The Output comment at the end of the code shows the three swapped pairs.

Think of T as a blank in a form. The function says "give me two things of the same kind, whatever kind that is". Each call fills in the blank. The name T is only a habit; you could call it Item or anything else.

A generic function can only do what it is sure every possible T can do. swap_pair only moves values around, which works for every type. Comparing two values with > does not work for every type (what would it mean to compare two files?). So this does not compile:

The fix is to tell Rust that T must be a type that can be compared. You do that by writing T: PartialOrd. PartialOrd is a trait (a named ability) that types with < and > have. Read T: PartialOrd as "any type T, as long as it can be ordered". The next lessons explain traits and these bounds properly; for now just copy the pattern.

&[T] is a slice of any type T. Looping over a reference to a slice gives a reference to each item, just like looping over &prices did with a Vec. The function returns a reference to the biggest item, so it never copies or moves anything. It panics on an empty slice, because items[0] does not exist.

Generics have no run-time cost. The compiler makes a separate copy of the function for each type you really use (this is called monomorphization), so largest::<i32> runs as fast as a hand-written i32 version. This is closer to C++ templates than to Java generics, which erase the types. Rust checks the whole function body once, using only the bounds, whereas C++ checks the parts that depend on T only when each use is expanded.

exercise.prompt: last_item only works on slices of i32. Make it work for slices of any type, so it also works on a list of words. Then, at the end of main, make an array of three words (red, green and blue) and print its last item. It should print two lines: 15 and blue. Hint: fn last_item<T>(items: &[T]) -> &T, and let words = ["red", "green", "blue"];

quiz.question: What does the <T> in fn swap_pair<T>(...) do?
options: Declares T as a new struct that the function builds every time it runs
Declares T as a constant whose value is fixed when the program starts
Declares T as a placeholder that stands for a real type, chosen at each call

quiz.question: Why does largest need T: PartialOrd?
options: Because > only works on types that can be ordered, and a bare T promises nothing
Because slices must be sorted before you can search them for the largest item
Because the function returns a reference, and references need PartialOrd

quiz.question: How does Rust decide which type T is when you call swap_pair(("a", "b"))?
options: It uses i32 unless you write another type in angle brackets at the call
It works T out from the types of the arguments you pass
It decides at run time, after looking at the values
